title: About Onim
excerpt: A free library of 4,041 calculators and 19 file tools across fifteen sections — who does what, how each answer is checked, and what the site does with what you type.
content:
Onim is a free collection of 4,041 calculators and 19 browser-based file tools — 4,060 tools in all — organised into fifteen sections. Calculators are one section of this site, not the whole of it: the same catalogue that holds the Math, Finance and Physics calculators also holds the Audio, Video, Image, PDF, Developer, Converter, Security, Gaming, Compressor, Productivity, Design & CSS, Text & Writing, Art & Color and Social & Community tools. You pick a section, you pick a tool, and the page shows the formula or the method that produced the answer. No account, no paywall, no "unlock the result" step.

One site, fifteen sections

The site is not a calculator website with a tools page bolted on, and it is not a file-tools website either. It is a library in which calculators are one category. The fifteen sections are:

  • Calculators — 4,041 pages across Biology, Chemistry, Construction, Conversion, Ecology, Everyday life, Finance, Food, Health, Math, Physics, Sports, Statistics and Other. Every page has inputs, a result and the equation it used.
  • Audio Tools, Video Tools, Image Tools, PDF Tools, Developer Tools, Converters, Security Tools, Gaming Tools, Compressors, Productivity Tools, Design & CSS Tools, Text & Writing Tools, Art & Color Tools, Social & Community Tools and Fun & Random Tools — 19 working tools that take a file, a link or a snippet of text and give you back something usable. They run in the browser: the file you hand over is never uploaded.

Every section has the same furniture, so moving from a loan calculator to a video frame grabber does not feel like changing sites: a searchable list of that section's tools, a "browse all" index, and a card for each tool that states what it does in one sentence.

Why the calculator pages are built the way they are

A calculator that only prints a number is a black box, and a black box is not much use when the number matters. Each calculator is described by the relationships between its inputs. Those equations are what the page runs on — once on the server while the page is drawn, and again in your browser the moment you press Calculate, so the two can be compared. Where a problem needs more than arithmetic (a table lookup, an iterative solve, a piecewise rule, a tax band), that logic is written out step by step instead of being hidden.

Every calculator page therefore carries the same parts: the formula with its variables defined, a worked example with real numbers, the assumptions the answer rests on, a table of neighbouring results, a short article on what the result means and where people get it wrong, and the questions readers actually ask about it.

How the tools are built

The file tools are written to do one job properly rather than many jobs approximately. An image compressor that changes the dimensions is not a compressor, and a converter that silently re-encodes your audio is worse than one that refuses. Where a tool cannot do something exactly — a PDF that will not extract as editable text, a colour profile that has no browser-side equivalent — the page says so before you run it, in the same place you would have found the "Start" button.

Everything that can stay on your device does. Files are read with the browser's own APIs, processed in the page and handed back for download. Nothing is posted to a server, and nothing is kept after you close the tab.

How the answers are checked

Each calculator is tested against worked examples whose results are stated independently of the code: the answer is computed by hand or taken from an authoritative source, then the page has to reproduce it. A calculator that disagrees with its worked example is a bug, and it is fixed rather than annotated. Every field is tested with numbers below and above its sensible range, letters are refused with a message under the field rather than a silent zero, and every result is checked for its unit and rounded to no more than three decimals.

File tools are tested on files with known properties — a 1200-pixel image that has to come back 1200 pixels wide, a PDF whose page count must not change, an audio file whose duration is the same after conversion. The tests run on every release, on the live site as well as locally.

Who does what

Onim is written and maintained by a small independent team, and every page has exactly three jobs behind it: someone writes it and checks that the prose matches the formula, someone builds the solver or the tool and keeps it running, and someone checks the subject against a published source before it goes live. The same person often does two of them, which is why a calculator that is wrong is usually fixed the same week it is reported.

Editorial

Calculators and articles

Writes the explanation behind every calculator page: the formula with its variables defined, the worked example, the assumptions the answer rests on, and the part that says where people go wrong. Reads each draft against the equation rather than against the previous draft.

The test a page has to pass: it should be able to explain its own answer to someone who has put the calculator away.

Engineering

File tools and platform

Builds the browser-side tools, the calculator solver, the search and the pages themselves. The rule applied to a file tool is that it does the one job it claims and refuses rather than guesses — a converter that silently re-encodes is a bug, not a feature.

Reads every bug report that arrives through the contact form, usually before anyone else sees it.

Review

Health, biology and chemistry

Checks the results that people act on against primary sources and clinical convention, and signs off the numbers that go into the worked examples. Where a formula has more than one convention — a calorie, a tonne, a definition of normal — the page has to say which one it uses.

The rule for a result someone might act on: if a careful reader could misread it, it is worded wrongly.

The three portraits and the workspace photograph on this page are illustrative images made for Onim, not photographs of named individuals. They are labelled as such, and the AI policy says how images on the site are produced. Nothing on this site publishes a testimonial, a reviewer or a user that does not exist.

How we work, and how you can tell

Every page states when it was last updated, and the calculators are revised when a formula, a unit convention or a tax rule changes. Corrections are made to the page, not appended in a footnote, and a page that disagrees with its own worked example is treated as broken until it is fixed.

If a page is wrong, the fastest way to have it corrected is to tell us what you entered, what you got and what you expected — the contact page takes all three. Reviews on calculator pages come from readers and are published under the name the reader chose; none of them is written by us.

What happens to what you type

Calculations run in your browser and on this server while the page is being drawn. We do not store your inputs into a calculator, we do not build profiles from them, and we do not sell data to anyone. Uploaded files are read in your browser and never leave it. The only information we keep is what you deliberately send — a message through the contact form, a name attached to a review, or a like on a page — and each of those is described in the privacy policy, which also says how to have it removed.

How the site is paid for

Onim is free to use and costs money to run. It is funded by advertising: a small number of clearly marked placements, never inside a result and never between you and an answer. Advertisers do not see the values you enter, cannot influence a result, and get no access to the calculators themselves. If advertising is switched off on this deployment, nothing else about the site changes.

Why we write policies in plain language

A site that asks you to trust its arithmetic should be equally clear about what it does with your data, what it will not do with your files, and where it stops being an authority. That is why Privacy, Cookies, AI policy, Terms and Disclaimer are written as pages a reader can actually finish, rather than as boilerplate. They describe this site as it is: a free tool library, run by three people, funded by ads, storing almost nothing.

How this page was made

Some drafting and code review on this site is AI-assisted; the formulas, worked examples and review passes are written and checked by a person, and the AI policy says exactly which parts that applies to and which it does not. The images on this page were generated for Onim rather than licensed from a stock library, which is why they are labelled as illustrative rather than presented as photographs of the team.

Getting in touch

Bug reports, corrections and requests all go to the same place. If a result looks wrong, the calculator name, the values you entered and the answer you expected is usually enough to reproduce it. Requests for a calculator or a file format are read, and a good share of what is on the site today started as one of those messages.
